To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the crotonase orthologous to rat mitochondrial crotonases in Pseudomonas genomes catalyzes the hydration of a 3-methylglutaryl CoA derivative and that it does so using a single glutamate residue that functions as the catalytic base.

(i) a new member of the crotonase family, (3S)-MGCH, has been discovered that uses a different catalytic mechanism to hydrate an enoyl-Coa and (ii) the catalytic mechanism is unique among the crotonase enzymes and is an example of opportunism in which the gamma-carboxyl group of the substrate is functionally equivalent to one of the two active site glutamate carboxylates of the other members.
(1) MGCH catalyzes hydration of (E)-enoyl-CoA using Glu164 but without Glu144 and (2) the gamma-carboxylates of substrates functionally replace the missing Glu144.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the discovery of new members of the crotonase family of enzymes and the characterization of their catalytic mechanisms.
the evolution of function in the enoyl CoA hydratase superfamily.

the evolution of function in the enoyl-coenzyme A hydratase superfamily and the discovery of the first hydratase that uses only one of the two active site glutamates that are conserved in all members of the superfamily.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the bacterial MGCHs are members of the crotonase family that use only one active site glutamate to catalyze a reaction that is different from the reactions catalysed by the paradigm crotonase and by mammalian MGCH.
bacterial MGCH is the only known hydratase that utilizes a single active-site glutamate residue for catalysis.
bacterial MGCH is a member of the crotonase family that utilizes a single glutamate in the oxyanion hole to catalyze the syn-hydralation of (3S)-3-methyl-glutaconyl-CoAs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MGCHs have evolved from the crotonase fold by a combination of gene duplication and gene loss events, with the latter resulting in a reduction to a single catalytically important residue.
bacterial MGCH and eukaryotic crotonase have evolved different strategies to synthesize (3S)-HG-CoA from (E)-3MG-CoA, and that the bacterial MGCH strategy is the simpler of the two.

MGCHs have evolved in different ways in bacteria and eukaryotes, with bacterial enzymes utilizing a single active site residue to catalyze a reaction that is catalyzed by two residues in the eukaryotes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the crotonase fold has evolved to perform a variety of different reactions by using the same catalytic strategy.
the catalytic strategies of the members of the superfamily are not as rigid as once thought.
the catalytic strategy of the crotonase scaffold is sufficiently versatile to accommodate different combinations of residues that catalyze different reactions.
